package_inventory.notes: lakefile.toml declares only mathlib, so there is no non-Mathlib package inventory to record for the Chapter 1 external-source research completed so far.

sources.citation: Andrew V. Sutherland, 18.785 Number Theory I, Lecture #1: Absolute values and discrete valuations (MIT, Fall 2021).
sources.reason: This is the closest statement-level match to the opening-batch blobs: it contains the introduction, the absolute-value definitions, the nonarchimedean criterion, the p-adic definition, Ostrowski's theorem, and the product formula in essentially the same form as the transcribed lecture.
formalization_leads: Use this as the canonical prose reference when Stage 3 formalization needs the exact wording or surrounding context of the opening batch, including the introduction's FTA / maximal-ideal / number-field-presentation / F_q[t] comparison sentences.
It confirms that Lemma 1.4, Theorem 1.8, and Theorem 1.9 are intentionally deferred to Problem Set 1 rather than proved in the lecture notes.

sources.citation: Andrew V. Sutherland, 18.785 Number Theory I, Problem Set #1 (MIT, Fall 2021).
sources.reason: This source contains the exact proof obligations omitted from the lecture: the nonarchimedean characterization in Lemma 1.4, Ostrowski's theorem on Q, and the product formula on Q.
formalization_leads: Treat it as the primary natural-language proof source for the current Mathlib gaps around Lemma 1.4 and the product formula on Q.
Its parallel F_q(t) exercises are useful for keeping the lecture's number-field and function-field analogies aligned in later formalization.

sources.citation: Andrew V. Sutherland, 18.785 Number Theory I, Lecture #9: Local fields and Hensel's lemmas (MIT, Fall 2021).
sources.reason: The introduction frames local fields as completions of global fields, and these later notes supply that completion-to-local-field background in the same course vocabulary.
formalization_leads: Use it when later blobs need the precise local-field facts alluded to in the introduction's discussion of R and Q_p.
It gives the natural follow-on source for completion and valuation-ring language that reappears after the opening batch.

sources.citation: Andrew V. Sutherland, 18.785 Number Theory I, Lecture #13: Global fields and the product formula (MIT, Fall 2021).
sources.reason: These notes revisit the same place/completion language from the opening lecture and then package the product formula in the broader global-field setting, which is useful once the local Q result is formalized.
formalization_leads: Use it to normalize terminology around places, completions, and finite versus infinite places before writing later reference blobs.
It provides the clearest course-internal bridge from the opening-batch Q statements to the later global-field product-formula formalization.

sources.reason: The lecture explicitly cites Serre as a reference for much of Section 1.2, so this is the natural book-level source for the absolute-value background, p-adic constructions, and surrounding local-field context.
formalization_leads: Use it when later stages need a durable book reference rather than course-specific notes for the opening-batch absolute-value material.
It is the best source in the lecture bibliography for filling in background that the lecture states but does not prove.

sources.citation: Andrew V. Sutherland, 18.785 Number Theory I, Lecture #1: Absolute values and discrete valuations (MIT, Fall 2021).
sources.reason: The middle-batch blobs are transcribed almost verbatim from pages 4-5 of this lecture, including the valuation and DVR definitions, the Z_(p) and k((t)) examples, the DVR characterization theorem statement with its deferred proof citation, and the integral-extension discussion through Proposition 1.18 and Definition 1.19.
formalization_leads: Use this as the canonical statement-level source for the entire middle batch before consulting broader commutative-algebra references.

It confirms that Theorem 1.16 is intentionally deferred to bibliography references [1, Section 23] and [2, Chapter 9], while Proposition 1.18 is meant to be proved by the symmetric-polynomial argument stated here.

sources.citation: Andrew V. Sutherland, 18.785 Number Theory I, Lecture #8: Complete fields and valuation rings (MIT, Fall 2021).
sources.reason: These later course notes revisit valuation rings and DVRs from the localization/completion perspective used in the rest of the course, so they are the best course-internal continuation source once the introductory statements from Lecture 1 need downstream context.
formalization_leads: Use this when later reference blobs need the connection between DVRs, localizations at primes, and completions that is only hinted at in the middle batch.
It gives the same course vocabulary for moving from the elementary valuation-ring examples to local-field formalization.

sources.citation: The Stacks Project, Section 10.50: Valuation rings.
sources.reason: This gives a freely accessible commutative-algebra reference for the valuation-ring criterion, locality, value groups, the associated valuation, and the characterization of valuation rings via principal finitely generated ideals.
formalization_leads: Use Lemmas 10.50.4-10.50.5 and 10.50.12-10.50.15 as the cleanest prose guide for rebuilding the valuation-ring facts that the lecture states without proof.

It is especially useful when Stage 3 needs a source for proving that the valuation ring attached to a valuation is local and for comparing the abstract valuation-ring definition with the valuation-theoretic one.

sources.citation: Allen Altman and Steven Kleiman, A Term of Commutative Algebra, Chapter 23: Discrete valuations, Worldwide Center of Mathematics, 2013.
sources.reason: Reference [1, Section 23] cited in the lecture bibliography develops discrete valuations, valuation rings, uniformizers, and the standard DVR characterizations in the exact commutative-algebra range needed for the middle batch.
formalization_leads: Use Chapter 23 as the main deferred-proof source for Theorem 1.16, especially for the equivalence between DVRs, local PIDs, and one-dimensional normal local rings.
Its valuation-first development is also a good backup source for the lecture's claims about units, ideals, and generators in a DVR.

sources.citation: M. F. Atiyah and I. G. Macdonald, Introduction to Commutative Algebra, Chapter 9: Discrete valuation rings and Dedekind domains, Addison-Wesley, 1969.
sources.reason: Reference [2, Chapter 9] cited in the lecture bibliography is the standard short source for local-domain/DVR equivalences and the ideal-theoretic structure of DVRs that underlies Theorem 1.16.
formalization_leads: Use Proposition 9.7 and the surrounding chapter as the second deferred-proof source for Theorem 1.16 when the lecture's bibliography is followed literally.
This source is also useful for the localization example Z_(p) and for matching the lecture's PID, local, and dimension-one characterizations against a standard text.

sources.citation: The Stacks Project, Section 10.18: Local rings.
sources.reason: This supplies a stable, freely accessible reference for the basic definitions of local rings and residue fields, together with the localization example used in Example 1.14.
formalization_leads: Use it when later scaffolding needs an explicit source for the local-ring and residue-field terminology that the lecture treats as standard background.
It is the quickest prose reference for identifying the maximal ideal and residue field of a localization.

sources.citation: The Stacks Project, Section 10.36: Finite and integral ring extensions.
sources.reason: This section gives a direct definition of integral elements and proves that the set of elements integral over a base ring is a subalgebra, matching exactly the mathematical content of Definition 1.17, Proposition 1.18, and Definition 1.19.
formalization_leads: Use Lemmas 10.36.4-10.36.7 as the cleanest replacement for the lecture's algebraic-closure argument when formalizing closure of integral elements under addition and multiplication.
Definition 10.36.9 is the exact prose model for the integral-closure definition in 1.19, and Lemma 10.36.11 is the natural next source once localization of integral closure becomes relevant.

sources.citation: Andrew V. Sutherland, 18.785 Number Theory I, Lecture #1: Absolute values and discrete valuations (MIT, Fall 2021).
sources.reason: These notes are the exact prose source for the tail batch: they contain the same sequence of results on transitivity of integrality, integrally closed rings, valuation rings, number fields, rings of integers, and the two quadratic examples.
formalization_leads: Use this as the canonical statement-level reference when Stage 3 formalizes the tail batch, especially for the valuation-ring proof and the explicit quadratic witnesses (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2 and (1 + sqrt(7)) / 2.
The notes also identify which arguments are meant to be textbook citations rather than in-lecture proofs, which helps distinguish proof scaffolding from external dependencies.

sources.citation: Allen Altman and Steven Kleiman, A Term of Commutative Algebra, Worldwide Center of Mathematics, 2013.
sources.reason: The book is cited explicitly in Proposition 1.20, and its integral-dependence chapter is the direct external source for transitivity of integrality in towers and the resulting integrally-closed corollary.
formalization_leads: Use the proof strategy behind Theorem 10.27 when a downstream formalization needs an unbundled tower argument rather than invoking Mathlib's ready-made `isIntegral_trans` lemma.
This source is also the most natural prose backup for showing that the integral closure of A in B is already integrally closed in B.

sources.citation: Michael F. Atiyah and Ian G. Macdonald, Introduction to Commutative Algebra, Addison-Wesley, 1969.
sources.reason: Chapter 5 is the lecture's other explicit citation for Proposition 1.20, and it also collects the surrounding commutative-algebra background on integral dependence, integrally closed domains, valuations, and minimal-polynomial arguments used across the tail batch.
formalization_leads: Use Corollary 5.4 as the prose source for transitivity of integrality and the associated closure argument in Corollary 1.21.

Its Chapter 5 discussion is also a compact reference for the rational-root style proof that UFDs are integrally closed and for the integrally-closed/minimal-polynomial criterion behind Proposition 1.28.

sources.citation: Andrew V. Sutherland, 18.783 Elliptic Curves, Lecture #12 (MIT, Fall 2025).
sources.reason: These notes give a clean standalone treatment of orders in finite-dimensional Q-algebras and prove that the ring of integers O_K is the unique maximal order, which is exactly the background compressed into Remark 1.27.
formalization_leads: Use the lattice-based proof that every element of an order is integral to justify the remark that every order sits inside O_K.
This is the best source in the current search pass for later Stage 3 work on the order/maximal-order language that Mathlib only partially packages.

sources.reason: The lecture bibliography names Serre as the durable background text for the local and valuation-theoretic material surrounding valuation rings and rings of integers, even when the lecture itself gives only a short proof sketch.
formalization_leads: Use it as the long-form background source for valuation-ring terminology and for the local-field perspective implicit in the discussion after Example 1.24.
It also provides a book-level reference for the notation O_K and the arithmetic role of rings of integers once formalization moves beyond the lecture's introductory examples.
